reference.source: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: An inherited disorder of bilirubin conjugation caused by deficient hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferase 1A1 (UGT1A1) activity
It produces unconjugated (indirect) hyperbilirubinaemia with otherwise normal liver enzymes and no haemolysis or biliary obstruction
Type 1 reflects virtually absent enzyme activity, causing severe unremitting jaundice from birth and a high risk of kernicterus
Type 2 (Arias syndrome) reflects markedly reduced but residual activity, with milder jaundice that characteristically falls in response to enzyme-inducing therapy
A reduction in bilirubin after an enzyme-inducer challenge helps distinguish type 2 from type 1, in which such a response is absent
Type 1 management relies on intensive phototherapy to keep bilirubin in a safe range, with liver transplantation being the definitive cure
It is distinguished from the milder, common Gilbert syndrome, which also involves reduced UGT1A1 activity but does not cause dangerous bilirubin levels
reference.pathophysiology: Bilirubin produced from haem breakdown must be conjugated with glucuronic acid by the hepatic enzyme UDP-glucuronosyltransferase 1A1 before it can be excreted in bile. In Crigler-Najjar syndrome, biallelic mutations in UGT1A1 abolish (type 1) or severely reduce (type 2) this enzyme activity, so unconjugated bilirubin cannot be efficiently processed and accumulates in the blood. Because unconjugated bilirubin is lipid soluble it can cross the blood-brain barrier, and at high concentrations it deposits in the basal ganglia and brainstem, causing bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus). The liver is otherwise structurally normal with no cholestasis or hepatocellular injury.
additionalDifferentials: Physiological and breast-milk jaundice of the newborn
Dubin-Johnson and Rotor syndromes (conjugated, distinguishing them)
Drug-induced inhibition of bilirubin conjugation or uptake
additionalInvestigations: Fractionated bilirubin confirming predominantly unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
Haemolysis screen including blood film, reticulocytes, and haptoglobin to exclude haemolytic causes
Otherwise normal liver enzymes and synthetic function to exclude hepatocellular or cholestatic disease
Response of serum bilirubin to an enzyme-inducer challenge to separate type 2 from type 1
Analysis of bile bilirubin conjugates where specialised testing is available
redFlags: Rising unconjugated bilirubin with lethargy, hypotonia, or abnormal tone signalling impending kernicterus
Failure of bilirubin to respond to intensive phototherapy
Intercurrent illness, fasting, or drugs precipitating a sharp rise in bilirubin
Progressive loss of phototherapy efficacy as skin surface area increases with growth
reference.prognosis: Type 2 disease is generally compatible with a normal life expectancy and low neurological risk when managed appropriately, whereas untreated type 1 carries a high risk of kernicterus and death; sustained phototherapy delays complications, and liver transplantation offers definitive correction of the enzyme defect.
pitfalls: Confusing severe Crigler-Najjar with benign Gilbert syndrome and underestimating kernicterus risk
Failing to appreciate that phototherapy becomes progressively less effective with age and growth
Prescribing drugs that displace bilirubin from albumin or that are conjugated by the same pathway
Delaying liver transplantation assessment in type 1 disease
Overlooking precipitants such as fasting, infection, or stress that acutely worsen jaundice
references: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
management: In type 1, rely on intensive phototherapy to keep unconjugated bilirubin within a safe range and prevent kernicterus
In type 2 (Arias syndrome), use enzyme-inducing therapy with phenobarbital to upregulate residual UGT1A1 and lower bilirubin
Reserve liver transplantation as the definitive cure for type 1 disease
Use exchange transfusion for acute dangerous rises in bilirubin or early signs of encephalopathy
Avoid recognised precipitants including fasting, dehydration, intercurrent illness and bilirubin-displacing drugs
Monitor serum bilirubin with neurological and auditory (brainstem response) surveillance for bilirubin toxicity
Provide genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive UGT1A1 disorder with family testing
